subs: Our toy cell has only three genes: A pushes up B, B pushes up C, and C holds back A.
Under each gene is a bar showing how much of its protein there is.
Last time I left you a question: what if we switch off C instead of B, so the cell stops making protein C?
What happens to A and B?
Here's the answer: C falls to 0.
A rises to 2, just like when we switched off B.
B rises too, but not to 2.
It stops at 1.6.
Why exactly 1.6?
Why does A reach 2, while B doesn't?
In this episode, we'll work it out ourselves, using nothing but arithmetic.
At the end of Episode 1, there were four boxes around this machine, and I didn't read them out.
They're the four big questions about a virtual cell: how do we describe a cell's state
what can we do to a cell
how do we build the machine
and how do we test whether it's right.
Today is box three: how the few rules inside the machine turn into numbers.
Let's start with a single bar.
Remember from Episode 1: a cell keeps making proteins, and it also keeps breaking them down.
It's a lot like a bathtub.
The tap pouring water in is production.
The drain letting water out is breakdown.
How fast is breakdown?
Think about it this way: over a short stretch of time, each protein has roughly the same chance of being broken down by the cell.
So if there are twice as many proteins, twice as many get broken down in the same stretch of time.
In other words, twice as much means twice as fast.
That's how we set up the toy, and in real cells, many proteins behave roughly like this.
In our toy, breakdown speed is simply the amount right now, times 1.
If the bar is at 1, right now it's losing 1 per unit of time
at 2, it's losing 2.
The unit of time is just the toy's clock.
It doesn't match any number of minutes or hours in a real cell.
The rule is simple: if more comes in than goes out, the bar rises
if less, it falls
if they're equal, it stops.
Turn on the tap, and the bar starts to rise.
The higher it gets, the faster water flows out.
It keeps rising until out matches in, and then the bar stops.
That's what Episode 1 meant by "balance out".
One careful point: "losing 1 per unit of time" is how fast it's going right now.
It doesn't mean the bar is empty after one unit of time.
It's like a speedometer reading 60: that doesn't necessarily mean you'll cover 60 miles in the next hour.
A car's speed is controlled by the driver.
Here, though, breakdown speed depends on the bar's own height: as the bar drops, breakdown slows down with it.
Since breakdown is just the height times 1, a bar stops at a height equal to its production speed.
Make 1 per unit of time, and the bar stops at 1
make 2, and it stops at 2.
So to find where a bar stops, all we need is how fast it's being made.
There's one way the bathtub isn't like a cell.
Water flows as one continuous body, so the level is smooth and steady.
Proteins are separate pieces you could count one by one, and when there are only a few, their number jumps around.
Our toy ignores that for now.
So what decides how fast production is?
The rules do.
Start with A: C holds back A.
Here's how the rule is written: A's production speed equals 2, times a "hold-back factor".
2 is how fast A is made at full power: 2 per unit of time.
The hold-back factor is a number between 0 and 1.
It says how much of that power is left right now: the harder A is held back, the smaller it gets.
The hold-back factor is a fraction.
The top is 1.
The bottom is 1 plus C times C.
Let's try a few numbers.
If C is 0, nothing holds A back: the bottom is 1, the factor is 1, full power.
If C is 1, the bottom is 2, and the factor is one half.
What about when C is 2?
Work it out yourself first.
The bottom is 1 plus 4, which is 5, so the factor is one fifth: only a fifth of the power is left.
The more C there is, the harder it holds A back.
In Episode 1, I said that C at its normal level cuts A's production in half, down to "half power".
That half comes right from here: normally C is 1, the factor is one half, so A's production speed is 2 times a half, which is 1.
That's why A stops at 1.
Switch off C, and C falls to 0.
The factor becomes 1, A's production speed is 2 times 1, which is 2, and A stops at 2.
Episode 1's "twice" is just 2 compared with 1.
When we switched off B, C also fell to 0, so A stopped at 2 that time too.
Now B: A pushes up B.
B's production speed equals 2, times a "push factor".
The push factor is a fraction too.
The top is A times A.
The bottom is 1 plus A times A.
Let's try numbers again.
If A is 0, the top is 0, the factor is 0.
Nothing pushes, and B isn't made at all.
If A is 1, it's one half: when A reaches 1, it pushes exactly halfway.
If A is 2, the top is 4 and the bottom is 5: four fifths, or 0.8.
After we switch off C, A is 2, so B's production speed is 2 times 0.8, which is 1.6.
B stops at 1.6.
That's the answer to last episode's question, worked out by hand.
What if there were more A?
In the toy, A never goes above 2, because its factor is at most 1.
So let's suppose we pour extra A protein into the cell from outside, and just use the formula to calculate.
Take a guess first: how big does A have to be for B to reach exactly 2?
Going from A = 2 to 3, B gains 0.2 and reaches 1.8.
Going to 4, it gains less than 0.1.
Even at A = 10, B is only 1.98.
Closer and closer, but it never reaches 2.
The reason is right there in the formula: the bottom is always 1 more than the top.
So no matter how big A gets, the push factor is always less than 1.
A bigger A only brings it closer to 1.
So B's production speed always stays below 2.
The closer you get to the top, the less each extra bit of push adds.
In our formula, however hard you push, you only get closer
you never touch it.
Scientists call this "saturation".
In chemistry, a saturated solution really has hit the top: add more, and it won't dissolve.
Here, saturation means getting closer and closer to the top, and always falling just short.
What they have in common: the further you go, the less each extra bit does.
Now we can answer the question from the start.
Holding back and pushing share the same ceiling: full power, 2.
The difference is whether you can reach it.
With holding back, once C really falls to 0, the factor is exactly 1, and A gets exactly to 2.
With pushing, you'd need infinitely much A to reach it.
With A at 2, the factor is only 0.8, so B stops at 1.6.
You might ask: why A times A, and not just A?
Let's compare.
With A alone, the factor is one third when A is 0.5, and two thirds when A is 2.
Multiply A by itself, and those become 0.2 and 0.8.
That makes small amounts count for less and large amounts count for more, so the push acts more like a switch.
But it isn't a real switch.
It doesn't jump all at once
it's a very steep slope.
The C times C on the hold-back side works the same way.
We chose these two formulas.
We chose them because quite a few real genes, when measured, show this same shape: flat, then steep, then flat again.
C's rule works just like B's: B pushes up C, so C's production speed is 2 times a push factor, only this time the factor uses B.
A pushes B, B pushes C, and C comes back to hold back A: the three rules join end to end into a loop.
Now let's go back to those three 1s from the normal state.
Put in A, B and C all equal to 1.
A's production speed: 2 times a half, which is 1.
B's: 2 times a half, 1.
C's: also 1.
All three bars are being made at speed 1, exactly matching their current heights, so every bar's production and breakdown balance out here, all at the same time.
That's why, normally, all three bars stop at 1.
In Episode 1, I said we'd "call that height 1".
Actually, we did it backwards.
We chose the numbers in the rules first: full power is 2, and the amount that pushes halfway is 1.
We chose them so the answer comes out exactly 1.
That keeps the arithmetic easy.
Switching off C is the same as changing the "2" in C's rule to 0: no more production.
The new state the machine is looking for is where, under the changed rules, every bar balances out again.
C has no production, so it falls to 0.
With C at 0, A stops at 2.
With A at 2, B stops at 1.6.
A drug works the same way.
Suppose a drug cuts A's full power in half.
That's changing the 2 in A's rule to 1.
That's what this episode adds to the machine: a perturbation, like switching off a gene or adding a drug, changes the rules, and the new state is where every bar balances out again.
But let's be clear: this time we could calculate one step after another because C went to 0, and that cut the loop open.
If the loop isn't cut, like with that drug, then when A changes, B and C change too, and that comes back to affect A.
You can't just calculate one step after another.
You could treat the three formulas as a set of equations and solve them together, but they're not the simple straight-line equations from school, and solving them is hard work.
Another way: start from some moment, and step forward a little at a time, to see where the bars end up.
That's next episode.
Exactly how much that drug lowers A, and whether it's exactly half, we'll work out in Episode 4.
Do real cells work like this?
Some parts do.
In the bacterium E.
coli, scientists took the stretch of DNA that controls how hard a gene works, and connected it to a protein that glows green: the faster the gene works, the faster the cell lights up.
Then they added a small molecule that gets this gene going.
The more they added, the faster the gene made its product, until it barely rose any more, staying flat at the top.
That curve is flat, then steep, then flat too, the same shape as the formulas we chose.
But there are differences too.
In our formulas, when nothing pushes, the factor is exactly 0.
That's why in Episode 1, after we switched off B, C had nothing pushing it and fell cleanly, all the way to 0.
A real gene with nothing pushing it often isn't completely shut off.
A little still leaks out.
When Episode 1 said "real cells wouldn't drop this cleanly", this is one of the reasons.
And in real cells, the numbers in these formulas aren't set by anyone: what full power is, how much it takes to push halfway, and how many times you multiply, which decides how steep the slope is.
They have to be measured in experiments, and only a tiny fraction have been measured carefully.
If you remember one sentence from this episode, make it this:
A bar stops where production and breakdown balance out
pushing saturates, and no amount of pushing reaches the top.
Here's a question to think about: imagine a brand-new toy cell, just starting up, with all three bars at 0.
Use today's three formulas: at that very moment, which bar is rising, and which ones aren't moving?
We'll reveal the answer at the start of the next episode.
